raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle BAC=60^\circ$ and $\angle ABC=45^\circ$. $AD$ bisects $\angle BAC$ and intersects $BC$ at point $D$. $P$ is a moving point on line $AB$. Connect $DP$ and construct parallelogram $DPQB$ with $DP$ and $DB$ as adjacent sides. Connect $CQ$. If $AC=6$, what is the minimum value of $CQ$?
raw_record.answer:
Solution: As shown in Figure 1, draw $CO \perp AB$ at $O$ and $DH \perp AB$ at $H$.

In $\triangle ACO$, $\angle CAB=60^\circ$,

$\therefore \angle ACO=30^\circ$,

$\therefore AO=\frac{1}{2}AC=3$,

$\therefore OC=\sqrt{AC^2-AO^2}=3\sqrt{3}$.

In $\triangle BCO$, $\angle CBA=45^\circ$,

$\therefore OB=CO=3\sqrt{3}$,

$\therefore AB=AO+OB=3\sqrt{3}+3$.

Since $AD$ bisects $\angle CAB$,

$\therefore \angle DAB=\frac{1}{2}\angle CAB=30^\circ$.

In $\triangle DHB$, $\angle CBA=45^\circ$,

Let $DH=HB=a$,

$\therefore AD=2DH=2a$,

$\therefore AH=\sqrt{AD^2-DH^2}=\sqrt{3}a$,

$\therefore AB=AH+BH=\sqrt{3}a+a$,

$\therefore \sqrt{3}a+a=3\sqrt{3}+3$,

$\therefore a=3$,

$\therefore DH=3$.

As shown in Figure 2, draw $QG \perp AB$ at $G$ and connect $DQ$ intersecting $AB$ at $M$.

Since quadrilateral $DPQB$ is a parallelogram,

$\therefore DM=QM$.

In $\triangle QGM$ and $\triangle DHM$,

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\angle QGM=\angle DHM=90^\circ \\
\angle QMG=\angle DMH \\
QM=DM
\end{array}\right.$,

$\therefore \triangle QGM \cong \triangle DHM$ (AAS),

$\therefore QG=DH=3$.

Hence, the distance from $Q$ to line $AB$ is always $3$.

Therefore, point $Q$ moves on a line parallel to $AB$, and the distance between the two lines is $3$.

When points $C$, $O$, and $Q$ are on the same line, $CQ$ is minimal.

The minimum value is $CO+3=3\sqrt{3}+3$.

Therefore, the answer is $\boxed{3\sqrt{3}+3}$.

Solution: As shown in Figure 1, draw $CO \perp AB$ at $O$ and $DH \perp AB$ at $H$.

In $\triangle ACO$, $\angle CAB=60^\circ$,

$\therefore \angle ACO=30^\circ$,

$\therefore AO=\frac{1}{2}AC=3$,

$\therefore OC=\sqrt{AC^2-AO^2}=3\sqrt{3}$.

In $\triangle BCO$, $\angle CBA=45^\circ$,

$\therefore OB=CO=3\sqrt{3}$,

$\therefore AB=AO+OB=3\sqrt{3}+3$.

Since $AD$ bisects $\angle CAB$,

$\therefore \angle DAB=\frac{1}{2}\angle CAB=30^\circ$.

In $\triangle DHB$, $\angle CBA=45^\circ$,

Let $DH=HB=a$,

$\therefore AD=2DH=2a$,

$\therefore AH=\sqrt{AD^2-DH^2}=\sqrt{3}a$,

$\therefore AB=AH+BH=\sqrt{3}a+a$,

$\therefore \sqrt{3}a+a=3\sqrt{3}+3$,

$\therefore a=3$,

$\therefore DH=3$.

As shown in Figure 2, draw $QG \perp AB$ at $G$ and connect $DQ$ intersecting $AB$ at $M$.

Since quadrilateral $DPQB$ is a parallelogram,

$\therefore DM=QM$.

In $\triangle QGM$ and $\triangle DHM$,

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\angle QGM=\angle DHM=90^\circ \\
\angle QMG=\angle DMH \\
QM=DM
\end{array}\right.$,

$\therefore \triangle QGM \cong \triangle DHM$ (AAS),

$\therefore QG=DH=3$.

Hence, the distance from $Q$ to line $AB$ is always $3$.

Therefore, point $Q$ moves on a line parallel to $AB$, and the distance between the two lines is $3$.

When points $C$, $O$, and $Q$ are on the same line, $CQ$ is minimal.

The minimum value is $CO+3=3\sqrt{3}+3$.

Therefore, the answer is $\boxed{3\sqrt{3}+3}$.

Reasoning: According to the coordinate/vector method, take AB as the x-axis, let A=(0,0), B=(L,0), and C be above AB. Because AC=6 and ∠BAC=60°, C=(6cos60°,6sin60°)=(3,3√3). Also because ∠ABC=45°, and from the figure BC slopes toward the upper left, the slope of line BC relative to horizontal AB is -1, that is, the equation of BC can be written as y=-(x-L)=L-x. Substituting C=(3,3√3), get 3√3=L-3, so L=3+3√3, that is B=(3+3√3,0).

AD bisects ∠BAC=60°, so AD forms a 30° angle with AB, and the slope is tan30°=1/√3, therefore the equation of AD is y=x/√3. D is the intersection point of AD and BC, so solving the equation x/√3=(3+3√3)-x gives x=3√3, y=3, therefore D=(3√3,3).

Let P=(t,0), because P moves on the straight line AB. The parallelogram DPQB takes DP and DB as adjacent sides, and according to the vector relationship there is Q=P+B-D. Therefore Q=(t,0)+(3+3√3,0)-(3√3,3)=(t+3,-3). So no matter how P moves, the y-coordinate of Q is constantly -3, that is, Q moves on the line y=-3.

Point C=(3,3√3), and the shortest distance to the line y=-3 is the perpendicular distance, namely 3√3-(-3)=3√3+3. This minimum value is attained when the x-coordinate of Q is 3; at this time CQ is perpendicular to the trajectory line of Q. Therefore the minimum value of CQ is 3√3+3.
